claims.sentence: DXA, also written DEXA, stands for dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, a scan that measures bone density.
claims.evidence: Trust page: "a special type of x-ray technology called dual energy x-ray absorptiometry"; quick and painless bone scan.

claims.sentence: The scan is used to help diagnose osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker.
claims.evidence: Basic definition; sources describe osteoporosis assessment and fracture risk. No specific page retrieved.

claims.sentence: The NHS lists DEXA among the tests that use X-rays.
claims.evidence: Retrieved NHS/trust text says DEXA uses low-dose X-rays; no text retrieved saying the NHS "lists" it among X-ray tests.
claims.newSentence: The NHS describes a DEXA scan as a test that uses low-dose X-rays.

claims.sentence: NHS 111 Wales says a scan may be offered to people over 50 who are at risk of osteoporosis.
claims.evidence: The NHS 111 Wales eligibility text was not retrieved. Trust pages say a doctor can refer someone who may be at risk; trust criteria differ (one starts at over 40, another over 50 with intermediate or high FRAX).
claims.newSentence: NHS trust pages say a doctor can refer a person for a DEXA scan if they may be at risk of osteoporosis, and the criteria differ between services.

claims.sentence: It also says people under 50 may be offered one if they have other risk factors, such as smoking or a previous broken bone.
claims.evidence: Only one trust referral form was retrieved listing current smoker and previous low-trauma fracture as ticked risk factors; no NHS 111 Wales text on under-50s.
claims.newSentence: One NHS trust referral form lists being a current smoker and having had a previous low-trauma fracture among the risk factors it asks about.

claims.sentence: A doctor usually makes the referral.
claims.evidence: Trust pages: referrals usually come from a GP or hospital consultant; people generally cannot self-refer.

claims.sentence: Results are combined with a fracture risk assessment rather than used alone.
claims.evidence: Guideline text: BMD results should not be reviewed in isolation; fracture risk tools such as FRAX combine density with other factors (NHS formulary guideline, RUH leaflet).

claims.sentence: The person lies on their back on a padded table.
claims.evidence: Lying on back on a flat X-ray table is supported; "padded" was not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The person lies on their back on a flat table.

claims.sentence: A scanning arm passes over the body, usually the hips and spine, and the images go to a computer.
claims.evidence: NHS text: arm passes slowly over the area, usually hip and lower spine. Nothing retrieved about images going to a computer.
claims.newSentence: A scanning arm passes slowly over the body, usually the hip and lower spine.

claims.sentence: The scan is painless and takes between about 5 and 15 minutes, depending on the sources and the body part scanned.
claims.evidence: Sources give different times: NHS "usually 10 to 20 minutes", trusts ~10 minutes, up to 15 minutes, ~1 minute per scan. "5 to 15" not in any retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: NHS pages describe the scan as quick and painless, and the time it takes varies between services.

claims.sentence: The dose is low.
claims.evidence: NHS: DEXA uses much lower radiation than a standard X-ray, about the same as natural exposure over roughly 3 days.

claims.sentence: A Royal Marsden leaflet describes the added risk as extremely small and says there are no side effects of bone density scanning.
claims.evidence: Royal Marsden leaflet not retrieved; the "extremely small" wording and "no side effects" are not in retrieved text. A Royal Brompton page gave a numerical risk but is not the cited source.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says a DEXA scan uses a much lower level of radiation than a standard X-ray, similar to what a person is exposed to naturally over about three days.

claims.sentence: The T-score compares a person's bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus (US source) and UK NHS formulary text: T-score compares density with a healthy young adult of the same sex.

claims.sentence: Scores fall into bands described as normal, low bone density (osteopenia) and osteoporosis, and the laboratory report shows the bands used.
claims.evidence: Normal/osteopenia/osteoporosis bands supported (WHO classification in NHS trust text), but "the laboratory report shows the bands used" not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Scores are grouped into bands described as normal, low bone density (osteopenia) and osteoporosis.

claims.sentence: Osteoporosis is diagnosed using the lowest T-score across the lumbar spine, the neck of the thigh bone and the total hip.
claims.evidence: ROS-attributed summary in an NHS formulary guideline: osteoporosis diagnosed by T-score in lumbar spine, femoral neck and sites, using the lowest value. Secondary source; total hip listed in US NOF-style guidance.

claims.sentence: The Z-score compares a person with others of the same age, and it is used mainly for premenopausal women, men under 50 and children.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus (US source): Z-score may be used if premenopausal, male under 50, or a child; compares with people of same age, sex, weight, ethnicity.

claims.sentence: A T-score does not decide treatment alone.
claims.evidence: Guideline text: BMD alone has high specificity but low sensitivity; results should not be reviewed in isolation.

claims.sentence: The Royal Osteoporosis Society says the decision to offer a medicine is based on the overall chance of breaking a bone in the next ten years, rather than only on bone density.
claims.evidence: The ROS page was not retrieved. Ten-year fracture probability appears in the NOGG-linked FRAX review, not attributed to ROS.
claims.newSentence: UK osteoporosis guidance uses a fracture risk tool such as FRAX, which estimates the chance of a broken bone over ten years from bone density and other risk factors, so bone density alone does not decide treatment.

claims.sentence: A DXA scan is painless: the person lies on a padded table while a scanning arm passes over the hips and spine.
claims.evidence: Painless supported; "padded table" not retrieved; hip and lower spine supported.
claims.newSentence: A DXA scan is painless: the person lies on a flat table while a scanning arm passes over the hip and lower spine.

claims.sentence: The radiation dose is low, and a Royal Marsden leaflet describes the added risk as extremely small.
claims.evidence: Royal Marsden leaflet not retrieved; NHS says much lower dose than a standard X-ray.
claims.newSentence: The radiation dose is low: the NHS says a DEXA scan uses a much lower level of radiation than a standard X-ray.

claims.sentence: The T-score compares bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus (US source): compares with a healthy young adult of the same sex.

claims.sentence: The decision to offer a medicine rests on the overall chance of breaking a bone in the next ten years, not on the scan result alone.
claims.evidence: Ten-year fracture risk idea is in FRAX/NOGG sources, but not the ROS page; "rests on" overstates.
claims.newSentence: Treatment decisions use an assessment of the overall chance of breaking a bone, not the scan result alone.

claims.sentence: A DXA scan measures bone density at the hip and spine using very low-dose X-rays. This guide covers who is offered one and what the T-score does and does not decide.
claims.evidence: "Very low-dose" not in sources (they say much lower than standard X-ray); "who is offered one" not established.
claims.newSentence: A DXA scan measures bone density, usually at the hip and lower spine, using low-dose X-rays. This guide covers who may be referred for one and what the T-score does and does not decide.

notes: The search tool returns summaries, not full page text, so the nhs.uk, NHS 111 Wales and ROS pages were not read directly. Royal Marsden leaflet and the ROS page were not retrieved. T-score/Z-score definitions rest on MedlinePlus (US). Extra facts: NHS trust pages (https://www.leedsth.nhs.uk/services/radiology/bone-density-scan-dexa/) say no special preparation is needed; metal fasteners may need removing; NHS says bone density scans are not recommended in pregnancy (https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/dexa-scan/what-happens/).
